text: The European Union (EU) Medical Device Regulation 2017/745 (EU MDR) The EU MDR aims to ensure a high level of protection of human health and safety and the proper functioning of the EU medical device market. It introduces stricter, more detailed requirements for clinical evaluation. Clinical evaluation is a systematic and ongoing process of collecting, appraising, and analyzing clinical evidence to verify the device’s safety, performance, and clinical benefits. It forms a core part of the conformity assessment procedure required for CE marking, demonstrating compliance with the General Safety and Performance Requirements (GSPRs) in Annex I and confirming that the device is suitable for its intended purpose. Article 61 Requirements Article 61 outlines the responsibilities of the manufacturer, the notified body (NB), and, where applicable, the expert panel. The manufacturer prepares a Clinical Evaluation Plan (CEP) defining scope, criteria, and methods, and a Clinical Evaluation Report (CER) documenting results and conclusions. The NB assesses both documents, while expert panels provide scientific advice for high-risk or innovative devices. Clinical evaluation must be performed by qualified, impartial personnel and be appropriate for the device’s intended purpose, risk class, target population, and expected clinical benefits. The evaluation must rely on sufficient, relevant, and scientifically valid clinical data from clinical investigations, clinical experience, scientific literature, or a combination thereof. Clinical Evaluation Principles The clinical evaluation follows a methodologically sound and transparent procedure aligned with MEDDEV 2.7/1 Rev. 4 and applicable MDCG guidance. It includes defining the scope and objectives, identifying and appraising clinical data, generating clinical evidence, and assessing safety, performance, and clinical benefits. The CER documents conclusions, limitations, evidence gaps, and the need for further clinical investigations or PMCF, and is updated throughout the device lifecycle. The manufacturer determines and justifies the level of clinical evidence necessary to demonstrate conformity with the GSPRs. Use of EU MDR Article 61(10) For certain devices, including accessories, manufacturers may apply Article 61(10) when non-clinical data alone such as performance testing, bench testing, and pre-clinical evaluation are sufficient to demonstrate conformity. This route does not apply to Class III or implantable devices. If clinical claims are made that imply clinical benefit, relevant clinical data must be generated and evaluated, and Article 61(10) no longer applies.

Expert Guidance Article 61(10) does not exclude available clinical data; rather, it applies when clinical data are not appropriate for demonstrating conformity. Literature screening remains necessary to identify risks and ensure state-of-the-art alignment in accordance with Annex III. The provision is not intended for devices lacking clinical data, but for devices where conformity can be demonstrated using robust non-clinical evidence.

As per the classification criteria set out in Annex VIII of Regulation (EU) 2017/745, the Double J Stent (Short Term) is intended for continuous use for a duration between 60 minutes and up to 30 days, and is therefore considered a short-term use device. The risk class of the device and the justification for the applicable classification rule have been determined in accordance with Annex VIII of the EU MDR. The Double J Stent (Short Term) is an invasive device introduced into the body via a natural orifice (urethra) and is intended for internal urinary drainage from the kidney to the bladder. In accordance with Rule 5 of Annex VIII, invasive devices with respect to body orifices intended for short-term use are classified as Class IIa. Therefore, the Double J Stent (Short Term) is classified as a Class IIa medical device under Regulation (EU) 2017/745.

The Double J Stent (Short Term) is a passive, implantable ureteral stent intended to support urine flow from the kidney to the bladder in cases of ureteral obstruction or impaired drainage. The mechanism of action is mechanical and is based on the following: 1. Internal Urinary Drainage The stent is placed within the ureter, extending from the renal pelvis to the urinary bladder. Its hollow tubular structure provides a conduit that allows urine to pass from the kidney to the bladder when normal ureteral flow is compromised. 2. Bypassing Ureteral Obstruction In medical conditions such as calculi, hydronephrosis, ureteral stricture, or post-procedural swelling, the stent maintains patency of the ureter by creating an open channel for urine passage. 3. Anchoring via Double J (Pigtail) Configuration The proximal and distal ends are shaped into pigtails (“Double J”) to anchor the device within the renal pelvis and bladder, thereby reducing the risk of migration. 4. Guidewire-Assisted Placement The stent is introduced over a compatible guidewire using a pusher system, allowing accurate positioning within the ureter. 5. Temporary Support Function The device is intended for short-term use (up to 30 days) and provides temporary mechanical support to ensure drainage until the underlying condition is resolved or further intervention is performed. Principle of Operation and Mode of Action Double J Stent is a thin, flexible plastic tube that is placed temporarily in the ureter to help urine drain from the kidney into the bladder in the case of a blockage.

The Double J Stent (Short Term) is intended to be used by qualified healthcare professionals trained and experienced in urological procedures. The intended users include: • Urologists • Surgeons trained in endourology or urological interventions • Interventional specialists performing ureteroscopic procedures • Trained operating room or catheterization laboratory personnel under physician supervision The device is intended for use in a clinical/hospital setting, including operating theatres, endoscopy suites, and other controlled healthcare environments. Proper knowledge of ureteral anatomy, guidewire-assisted placement techniques, and stent positioning is required for safe and effective use.

The Double J Stent (Short Term) is intended for internal urinary drainage from the kidney to the bladder in medical conditions such as ureteral obstruction, calculi, hydronephrosis, ureteral stricture, and during or after urological procedures. When used as intended, the device provides the following clinical benefits: 1. Maintenance of Ureteral Patency Provides a temporary internal conduit within the ureter to maintain patency and allow urine to pass from the kidney to the bladder. 2. Restoration of Urine Flow Supports continuous urinary drainage in cases where normal ureteral flow is compromised. 3. Relief of Obstruction-Related Symptoms Assists in managing conditions associated with impaired urinary drainage, such as hydronephrosis and obstruction due to calculi or strictures. 4. Support Following Urological Procedures Maintains drainage and ureteral alignment during the post-procedural healing phase following endourological interventions. 5. Temporary Short-Term Drainage Solution Provides short-term (up to 30 days) internal drainage support until the underlying condition is resolved or further definitive treatment is performed. The clinical benefits are achieved through mechanical maintenance of ureteral patency and are consistent with the established clinical practice for short-term ureteral stenting.

The Double J Stent (Short Term) is a sterile, single-use ureteral stent intended for short-term internal urinary drainage from the kidney to the bladder in conditions such as ureteral obstruction, calculi, hydronephrosis, ureteral stricture, pyeloplasty with UPJ obstruction, and residual renal calculi. The device is designed to maintain ureteral patency and support continuous urine flow for a duration of up to 30 days. It features a bilateral pigtail (Double J) configuration to reduce the risk of migration, tapered ends to facilitate guidewire-assisted placement, and multiple drainage openings along the shaft to enable effective urine passage. The device is radiopaque to allow visualization during placement. It is supplied sterile, intended for single use only, and is available with or without a polypropylene string to facilitate stabilization and removal. Kit variants include a pusher, guidewire, and clamp to assist in controlled insertion. The materials used are suitable for short-term internal use and have undergone biological safety evaluation, and the device is sterilized using a validated Ethylene Oxide (EtO) process. The Double J Stent (Short Term) is classified as a Class IIa medical device under Regulation (EU) 2017/745.

The use of the Double J Stent (Short Term), as with other ureteral stents, may be associated with certain foreseeable complications and adverse events. Based on the device description, intended use, and known risks associated with ureteral stenting procedures, the potential complications include: • Urinary tract infection (UTI) • Stent migration or malposition • Hematuria

Unlike a systematic literature review, it does not follow a fully pre-defined protocol for comprehensive searching, study selection, and critical appraisal, and therefore may not capture all available evidence. The included scientific articles collectively describe the medical condition addressed by the device, outlining its pathophysiology, clinical presentation, and epidemiological relevance. The literature consistently reflects current clinical practice and state-of-the-art management approaches, detailing standard treatment pathways, commonly used technologies, and their known limitations. The articles highlight key unmet clinical needs, including risks, complications, or performance constraints associated with existing therapeutic options, establishing the rationale for improved or alternative solutions. Evidence from the included publications also defines the typical target patient population, relevant comorbidities, and expected clinical outcomes associated with standard care. This clinical background provides a comprehensive, literature-supported context for assessing the device’s intended purpose, anticipated clinical benefits, and comparison against established therapeutic benchmarks within the current state of the art. Ureteral stents (commonly “Double J” stents) are routinely used in urological practice to maintain ureteral patency and support internal urinary drainage, particularly in the context of ureteral obstruction and peri-procedural management of urinary stone disease. Published evidence consistently shows that, while ureteral stents are clinically useful, stent-related morbidity is common, with urinary symptoms and pain affecting daily activities and health-related quality of life in a substantial proportion of patients; early work by Joshi et al. reported that stent symptoms can reduce functional capacity and patient utility/quality-of-life measures, highlighting the importance of patient counselling and careful stent indication. To enable standardized assessment of these patient-reported outcomes, the Ureteral Stent Symptom Questionnaire (USSQ) was developed and validated as a multidimensional instrument for evaluating stent-related symptoms and quality of life, and has since undergone linguistic validation for broader clinical and research use (e.g., Italian and French versions). Systematic reviews and meta-analyses examining stenting versus no stenting after uncomplicated ureteroscopy/ureteroscopic lithotripsy indicate that routine postoperative stenting does not necessarily improve key effectiveness outcomes (e.g., stone-free results) in uncomplicated cases, while stent-related symptoms remain a relevant burden; therefore, evidence supports a risk-based, indication-driven approach to postoperative stent placement rather than automatic routine use in all patients. In parallel, literature describing ureteroscopy-related ureteral injury has introduced structured assessment tools such as the Post-Ureteroscopic Lesion Scale (PULS) to grade ureteral lesions and improve consistency in reporting, which is relevant to understanding the procedural context in which stents are commonly placed.

The historical context summarizes the evolution of the medical condition’s management and the development of technologies historically used to address it. Published literature describes how clinical practice, treatment methods, and device technologies have progressed over time, including previously established approaches, their limitations, and the shift toward more advanced or safer solutions. The historical evidence highlights the maturity of the therapeutic area, demonstrating how clinical understanding and device performance expectations have evolved to align with the current state of the art. This context supports the justification for the device’s intended use by showing how the technology fits within the established clinical landscape and how it addresses limitations identified in earlier generations of treatment or device technologies. Ureteral stenting has evolved as a fundamental component of modern urological practice, particularly in the management of ureteral obstruction and peri-procedural urinary drainage. The concept of internal ureteral drainage emerged in the late 1960s and 1970s with the development of indwelling ureteral stents designed to maintain ureteral patency without the need for external drainage systems. The introduction of the Double J (pigtail) configuration, featuring curled proximal and distal ends, represented a major advancement by reducing stent migration and improving positional stability within the renal pelvis and bladder. This design has since become the standard configuration for ureteral stents worldwide. With the expansion of endourological techniques, particularly ureteroscopy and ureteroscopic lithotripsy for stone management, ureteral stents became widely used for postoperative drainage, prevention of obstruction due to edema, and facilitation of ureteral healing. Over time, clinical research shifted from establishing basic effectiveness to evaluating patient-reported outcomes, symptom burden, and quality of life associated with indwelling stents. Studies such as those by Joshi et al. (2003) highlighted the impact of stent-related symptoms, leading to the development of validated instruments such as the Ureteral Stent Symptom Questionnaire (USSQ) to systematically assess stent morbidity. Subsequent systematic reviews and meta-analyses examined the necessity of routine stenting following uncomplicated ureteroscopy, contributing to a more evidence-based, indication-driven approach to stent placement. This body of literature established the current understanding that ureteral stents provide clear clinical benefits in maintaining ureteral patency and supporting drainage, while also being associated with predictable and manageable side effects. Today, Double J stents remain the standard of care for short-term internal urinary drainage, with well-characterized performance, safety profiles, and recognized clinical applications in urology.

The device is intended for short-term use (up to 30 days), which further mitigates the likelihood of complications such as encrustation or blockage. Risk management activities conducted in accordance with applicable standards confirm that risks have been reduced as far as possible and that residual risks remain acceptable when weighed against the clinical benefits of maintaining ureteral patency and ensuring effective urinary drainage. Post-market surveillance data, as documented in the Technical File, do not indicate any unexpected safety concerns or trends that would alter the established benefit–risk profile. The review of the current scientific literature and clinical practice guidelines confirms that ureteral stenting, particularly using Double J–configured stents, represents an established and widely accepted method for short-term internal urinary drainage in patients with ureteral obstruction or following urological procedures. The Double J design, characterized by bilateral pigtail ends to reduce migration and a hollow lumen to maintain ureteral patency, is recognized as the standard configuration in contemporary urological practice. The analyzed literature demonstrates that ureteral stents are effective in restoring and maintaining urinary drainage and in supporting post-procedural ureteral healing. Reported side effects, including urinary tract infection, hematuria, irritative urinary symptoms, and occasional migration, are well characterized and consistent across studies. These effects are generally transient or manageable and are considered inherent to the device category rather than indicative of device malfunction when used as intended. The state-of-the-art review also indicates that while alternative management strategies exist (e.g., percutaneous nephrostomy or selective non-stenting in uncomplicated cases), internal ureteral stenting remains an appropriate and clinically justified intervention in indicated patients. Based on the available evidence, the Double J Stent (Short Term) aligns with the current state of the art in terms of design principles, intended use, safety profile, and clinical performance. The Double J Stent (Short Term) represents a well-established technology within the field of urology. Ureteral stents incorporating a bilateral pigtail (“Double J”) configuration have been in routine clinical use for several decades as a standard method for temporary internal urinary drainage. Since their introduction in the late 20th century, Double J ureteral stents have become an integral component of contemporary endourological practice for the management of ureteral obstruction, postoperative drainage following ureteroscopy or lithotripsy, and protection of ureteral integrity after reconstructive procedures. The fundamental design principle and clinical application of these devices have remained stable over time, and their safety and performance characteristics are extensively documented in scientific literature. The systematic reviews and meta-analyses included in the literature review (Haleblian et al., 2008; Nabi et al., 2007; Song et al., 2012) confirm that ureteral stents are widely accepted as effective devices for maintaining ureteral patency and preventing postoperative obstruction. These publications consistently demonstrate that stents provide reliable internal drainage when clinically indicated and are associated with predictable and manageable adverse effects. The literature further establishes that ureteral stenting is a common adjunct to ureteroscopy and stone management, reflecting its integration into the standard of care. Survey data (Auge et al., 2007) and expert discussions (Hughes et al., 2014) reinforce that ureteral stent placement is a routine clinical decision guided by patient and procedural factors, further supporting the maturity and established nature of the technology. The mechanism of action of the Double J Stent (Short Term) is purely mechanical and passive. The device maintains ureteral patency by providing a hollow conduit between the renal pelvis and bladder, thereby facilitating urine drainage and preventing obstruction due to ureteral edema, calculi fragments, or anatomical narrowing. The bilateral pigtail configuration at both ends of the stent serves as a retention mechanism to reduce migration and ensure positional stability. This mechanism of action has not changed over decades of use and is consistently described in the reviewed literature. No pharmacological, immunological, or metabolic mode of action is involved. The absence of an active component further supports the categorization of the device as a mature and well-characterized technology.

The safety profile of ureteral stents is similarly well established. The reviewed publications, including Joshi et al. (2003), demonstrate that irritative lower urinary tract symptoms, flank discomfort, and mild hematuria are common but generally transient and manageable during the indwelling period. Meta-analyses (Nabi et al., 2007; Song et al., 2012) report that while stent placement may increase postoperative urinary symptoms in some patient groups, serious adverse events remain uncommon. Additional case reports and clinical series included in the literature review describe complications such as encrustation, migration, obstruction, and fragmentation, particularly in the context of prolonged or forgotten stents. Importantly, these complications are strongly associated with extended indwelling duration beyond the intended short-term use rather than with inherent device design flaws. The predictable, time-dependent nature of these risks confirms that they are intrinsic to the device category and are adequately mitigated through appropriate patient selection, correct placement, and timely removal. The Double J Stent (Short Term) does not introduce novel materials, coatings, drug-eluting properties, or design features that would alter the established mechanism of action or risk profile of conventional ureteral stents. The materials used are established biocompatible polymers commonly employed in ureteral stent manufacturing and evaluated in accordance with ISO 10993 standards. The device does not present new clinical uncertainties compared to other marketed double pigtail ureteral stents. Therefore, from a technical, biological, and clinical perspective, the subject device aligns with the well-characterized device category described extensively in the literature. In accordance with Article 61(10) of Regulation (EU) 2017/745, a clinical investigation is not required where sufficient clinical evidence is available through existing literature, equivalence demonstration, post-market surveillance data, and risk management documentation. The systematic reviews, meta-analyses, observational studies, and case series included in the 12 selected articles collectively provide robust and consistent evidence regarding the safety, performance, and known side-effect profile of ureteral stents. The data demonstrate reproducible clinical outcomes and confirm that the benefit–risk profile of short-term ureteral stenting remains favorable when used as intended.

Considering the longstanding clinical history, stable and well-understood mechanism of action, predictable safety profile, absence of novel technological characteristics, and extensive supportive scientific literature, the Double J Stent (Short Term) fulfills the criteria of a Well-Established Technology (WET). The available clinical evidence is therefore sufficient to support conformity with the applicable General Safety and Performance Requirements (GSPRs) of Regulation (EU) 2017/745 without the need for a new pre-market clinical investigation. Ongoing post-market surveillance and periodic clinical evaluation updates ensure continued confirmation of safety and performance throughout the device lifecycle.

Based on the comparative assessment of technical, biological, and clinical characteristics, equivalence between the Biorad Double J Stent (Short Term) and the Cook Medical Double Pigtail Ureteral Stent has been established in accordance with the requirements of MDR Annex XIV (Part A) and MDCG 2020-5 guidance. Both devices share the same fundamental design concept (bilateral pigtail ureteral stent), operating principle (passive internal urinary drainage), and mechanical action (maintenance of ureteral patency). The materials used are established biocompatible polymers intended for short-term indwelling ureteral contact, with similar type and duration of tissue interaction and no intended pharmacological or biological mode of action. Clinically, both devices are intended for the same purpose—temporary internal drainage of the ureter in conditions such as obstruction or post-urological procedures—used in the same anatomical site, patient population, and by the same type of healthcare professionals. No clinically significant differences have been identified that would impact the safety or clinical performance of the subject device when compared to the selected marketed device. Therefore, it is concluded that the Biorad Double J Stent (Short Term) is equivalent to the Cook Medical Double Pigtail Ureteral Stent for the intended purpose, and the clinical data available for the equivalent device are applicable to support the clinical evaluation of the subject device.

The Double J Stent (Short Term) is classified as a Class IIa medical device in accordance with the classification rules set out in Annex VIII of Regulation (EU) 2017/745 (EU MDR), as it is an invasive device introduced into the body via a natural orifice and intended for short-term use. The conformity assessment procedure for the device has been carried out in accordance with Annex IX of the EU MDR (Conformity Assessment Based on a Quality Management System and Assessment of Technical Documentation). The manufacturer has established and maintains a Quality Management System compliant with Article 10(9) of the MDR and EN ISO 13485, covering design, manufacturing, final inspection, and post-market activities. The Technical Documentation has been prepared in accordance with Annex II and Annex III of the MDR and includes the device description and specifications, design and manufacturing information, risk management documentation, verification and validation data (including biological evaluation, sterilization validation, packaging validation, and performance testing), labeling and IFU, as well as the Clinical Evaluation Report prepared in accordance with Annex XIV (Part A). Literature Summary: This multicenter study evaluates the inter-rater reliability of the Post-Ureteroscopic Lesion Scale (PULS), a standardized grading system for ureteral lesions following ureteroscopy. Although the publication does not evaluate ureteral stents directly, it provides an important framework for consistent classification of ureteroscopic injury severity, which is relevant to clinical decision-making regarding postoperative measures such as ureteral stenting. The study supports the clinical background that ureteroscopic injury can vary in severity and that structured assessment improves consistency in reporting and management. From a CER standpoint, PULS is relevant as it helps contextualize stent use as part of post-procedural management strategies aimed at ensuring drainage and supporting ureteral healing when lesions are present. The publication therefore contributes indirectly to the state-of-the-art understanding of ureteroscopy-related risks and their relationship to stenting decisions.

The use of the Double J Stent (Short Term) has demonstrated a positive clinical impact in the management of ureteral obstruction and in providing temporary internal urinary drainage following urological procedures such as ureteroscopy, lithotripsy, and treatment of ureteral strictures or injuries. The primary therapeutic objective of the device is the restoration and maintenance of unobstructed urine flow from the renal pelvis to the bladder, thereby preventing hydronephrosis, relieving flank pain, and preserving renal function. From a safety perspective, although appropriate precautions are implemented, several factors may influence patient outcomes during ureteral stent placement. These include the patient's overall medical condition, age, anatomical considerations, presence of infection, and the indication for stenting. Procedural factors such as correct stent size selection, accurate positioning within the ureter, and adherence to aseptic technique are critical to minimizing complications. The device is supplied sterile and intended for single use; therefore, proper handling and strict compliance with the Instructions for Use (IFU) are essential to reduce risks such as infection or device malfunction. The clinical performance of the Double J Stent (Short Term) is dependent on appropriate patient selection and use according to the intended purpose. When properly placed, the stent maintains ureteral patency through its hollow lumen and pigtail retention design, reducing the risk of obstruction due to edema or residual stone fragments. Literature evidence confirms high technical success rates for placement and effective drainage in indicated patients. Recognized side effects associated with ureteral stenting include transient hematuria, lower urinary tract symptoms (frequency, urgency, dysuria), flank discomfort, and occasional urinary tract infection. Migration and encrustation are reported in the literature but are uncommon in short-term use and are strongly associated with prolonged indwelling duration. Severe complications are rare and typically related to delayed removal or improper use rather than inherent device design issues. Based on the cumulative evaluation of scientific literature, equivalence data, risk management documentation, and post-market surveillance findings, the Double J Stent (Short Term) demonstrates acceptable safety and clinical performance consistent with the current state of the art. When used as intended and in accordance with the IFU, the device provides effective short-term urinary drainage with a favorable benefit–risk profile.

The evaluation was conducted in accordance with Article 61 and Annex XIV (Part A) of the MDR and was based on a systematic review of scientific literature, demonstration of equivalence with a marketed Double Pigtail Ureteral Stent, device-specific verification and validation data, risk management documentation, and post-market surveillance information. Based on the cumulative assessment of available clinical evidence, the following conclusions are drawn: • The Double J Stent (Short Term) achieves its intended purpose of restoring and maintaining ureteral patency and facilitating temporary internal urinary drainage in indicated patients. • The device demonstrates a high technical success rate and predictable clinical performance consistent with the current state of the art. • The identified side effects—such as transient hematuria, irritative lower urinary tract symptoms, flank discomfort, urinary tract infection, migration, and encrustation—are well documented in the literature as inherent to the ureteral stent device category and are generally mild to moderate, manageable, and time-dependent.

• No new or unexpected safety concerns have been identified from the reviewed literature or post-market data. • The device does not compromise the clinical condition or safety of patients, users, or other persons when used in accordance with the Instructions for Use and within the intended short-term duration. • The overall benefit–risk profile is favorable, as the clinical benefits of relieving obstruction, preventing hydronephrosis, and preserving renal function outweigh the predictable and manageable risks associated with short-term ureteral stenting. In conclusion, the available clinical evidence confirms that the Double J Stent (Short Term) is safe and performs as intended for its defined clinical indications. The device is considered to comply with the relevant GSPRs of EU MDR 2017/745 throughout its intended lifetime.
